paragraphs: A reactive policy chooses actions from the agent’s current observed features. Those features may hide distinctions between underlying states, making the usual Markov assumption inappropriate. This paper studies how to learn the best reactive policy in a finite environment where observations are deterministic, so multiple underlying states can appear identical to the agent.

The proposed Committed Q-learning algorithm changes how the agent behaves while collecting experience. Upon entering an observed feature, it selects an action and keeps taking that action until the observed feature changes. Only then does it sample another action. This commitment rule is the central modification to classical Q-learning.

The authors prove almost-sure convergence to an optimal reactive policy under an assumption called rewire-robustness. They show this assumption is strictly weaker than the q-star realizability condition used previously. Their analysis introduces quasi-Markov environments to support the argument. The guarantee therefore expands the conditions under which reactive learning can be justified, while remaining conditional on a specific structural assumption.
icml-2026-commit-to-the-bit-reactive-rei.tldr: Committed Q-learning learns an optimal reactive policy under a weaker structural assumption by retaining its chosen action until the observed feature changes.

paragraphs: A saliency map highlights image regions that matter to a prediction, but highlighted pixels alone may not explain what the model recognizes. ConEx connects these spatial explanations to learned concepts, aiming to show both where a concept occurs and how it contributes to the model’s decision.

The framework automatically discovers concepts specific to each class and represents them with concept activation vectors. It learns these without manual concept supervision. An architecture-specific masking mechanism reduces noise introduced by segmentation masks, helping the learned concepts remain more coherent. The resulting explanations combine concept representations with saliency maps, connecting a prediction’s visual evidence to a more meaningful description of its components.

The authors also introduce Vector-Concept Match and Concept-Class Match, two complementary measures of concept alignment that support comparisons with other methods. Across the evaluated settings, ConEx reports state-of-the-art results on faithfulness, segmentation, and concept quality. These findings support evaluating explanations along several dimensions: whether they reflect model behavior, locate relevant image content, and organize that content into interpretable concepts.
icml-2026-conex-human-interpretable-sali.tldr: ConEx links automatically learned visual concepts to saliency maps, explaining where concepts appear and how they contribute to predictions.

paragraphs: This paper trains less computationally expensive machine-learned exchange-correlation functionals to reproduce a reference hybrid functional. The setting is hybrid distillation: semilocal models with cubic scaling learn B3LYP/def2-SVP targets associated with quartic-scaling hybrid calculations. The goal is to transfer the reference functional’s behavior into a cheaper approximation.

Derivative Informed XC-Loss adds supervision on first and second energy derivatives over admissible density matrices. These derivatives describe how energy responds to nearby changes. Matching them teaches the model local response behavior, beyond matching the final self-consistent solution. This gives training additional information about the shape of the reference energy function.

Across four architectures, the loss improves the main energy metrics, reducing total-energy mean absolute error by 66% when averaged uniformly across architectures. The density-sensitive energy metric also improves, although dipole and density errors do not improve uniformly. Distilled densities reduce hybrid self-consistency iterations by up to 55%. For downstream excited-state calculations, second-derivative supervision improves predictions, with XCdiff showing 24–35% lower mean excitation-energy error across molecule sizes on QM40.
icml-2026-derivative-informed-learning-o.tldr: Supervising energy derivatives improves cheaper learned approximations of a hybrid functional, with benefits for energy accuracy and downstream calculations.

paragraphs: When people adapt their features in response to a classifier, the decision rule also shapes their incentives. Some changes may be more desirable than others for ethical, economic, or institutional reasons. This paper asks how a decision maker can encourage desirable changes fairly across different agents while still pursuing predictive performance.

The framework brings together causal relationships between features, judgments about desirable changes, and disparities in information. It expresses the decision maker’s problem as constrained optimization, making fairness in desirable effort an explicit requirement. That formulation allows the cost of enforcing a chosen fairness tolerance to be studied alongside the original optimization objective.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees on the resulting loss in optimality for multiple broad classes of fairness measures. Experiments on real datasets also show a trade-off between classification accuracy and fairness in desirable effort. The contribution is a unified way to reason about these competing goals: a decision rule affects both predictions and how differently situated people are encouraged to change.
icml-2026-desirable-effort-fairness-and-.tldr: The paper formalizes how encouraging desirable changes fairly can trade off against a strategic classifier’s predictive objective.

paragraphs: Layer dropout skips layers during training, reducing computation and exposing a model to different effective depths. Despite earlier benefits in language and vision transformers, it has largely disappeared from large language model pretraining. This study investigates when layer dropout helps and how its configuration affects both training accuracy and later inference.

The authors jointly examine which layers are dropped, how dropout changes over training, and the optimizer settings. With suitable choices, they report lower or similar validation loss while saving up to 20% of training FLOPs. The result depends on configuring the training procedure appropriately; the paper’s contribution includes best practices and scaling analysis for doing so.

The trained models also support early exits, skipped intermediate layers, and self-speculative decoding, producing up to 1.4 times inference speedup with negligible accuracy loss. Evidence comes from more than 2,400 experiments, covering 271 million to 8.2 billion parameters and datasets up to 160 billion tokens. All pretraining experiments used Cerebras CS-3 systems, grounding the reported training results in that evaluated setup.
icml-2026-dont-drop-dropout-optimizing-l.tldr: Carefully configured layer dropout reduces LLM training computation and enables faster inference with little or no accuracy loss in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Explanations of model behavior often focus separately on model components, training examples, or training history. This separation can obscure how those factors interact. ExPLAIND combines all three within one framework and supports explanations at different levels of detail, connecting individual contributions to broader patterns in model behavior.

The method extends gradient path kernels to express models trained with AdamW as kernel machines. From the resulting feature maps, it derives influence scores for individual parameters and training steps. This gives a common mathematical basis for examining which parts of a model matter and when their influence develops during learning.

The authors validate the decomposition empirically and study two training processes. For a Transformer exhibiting grokking, their findings support previously proposed phases while describing the final phase as outer layers aligning around a representation pipeline learned after memorization. In EuroLLM pretraining, they find an initial phase dominated by outer-layer MLP learning, followed by greater relative influence from intermediate attention layers. These case studies show how unified attribution can refine descriptions of training dynamics.
icml-2026-explaind-unifying-model-data-a.tldr: ExPLAIND jointly attributes model behavior to components, data, and training history, revealing distinct learning dynamics in two case studies.

paragraphs: Sparse sketching reduces the arithmetic needed for randomized numerical linear algebra while retaining approximation guarantees. Its irregular pattern of nonzero entries, however, can cause scattered memory access on GPUs. This means a mathematically economical sketch may still use hardware inefficiently because memory bandwidth becomes difficult to exploit.

FlashSketch addresses this by designing the sketch and its implementation together. The authors introduce BlockPerm-SJLT, a family of sparse sketches structured for an optimized CUDA kernel. A tunable parameter controls the trade-off between GPU efficiency and sketching robustness. They establish guarantees within the oblivious subspace embedding framework and analyze how the parameter affects sketch quality.

Evaluations include standard randomized linear algebra benchmarks and GraSS, an end-to-end machine learning data attribution pipeline. Across the tested regimes and tasks, the method improves the available trade-offs between quality and speed. Its overall geometric-mean speedup is roughly 1.7 times that of prior state-of-the-art GPU sketches. The result illustrates why numerical algorithms and GPU memory access patterns benefit from being designed jointly.
icml-2026-flashsketch-sketch-kernel-co-d.tldr: FlashSketch co-designs sparse sketches and a CUDA kernel to improve sketching quality–speed trade-offs, reporting roughly 1.7 times geometric-mean speedup.

paragraphs: A buyer with a limited budget must choose what to purchase from sellers who have their own production costs and act strategically. Maximizing the value of purchased services is only one possible objective. This paper also studies buyer utility, which subtracts payments from value, and welfare, which subtracts production costs.

For welfare, the authors design a simple mechanism with a constant-factor approximation guarantee in the prior-free, worst-case setting. Utility behaves differently: prior-free mechanisms cannot offer a guarantee even with one seller. The paper therefore studies utility when the buyer knows probability distributions over sellers’ costs, making that information central to the available guarantees.

In this Bayesian setting, the authors first construct a utility-optimal mechanism whose spending respects the budget in expectation. They then modify it to respect the budget for every realization of seller costs while retaining near-optimal utility guarantees. Extensions cover further objectives. These distinctions matter because average budget compliance and guaranteed compliance in every outcome impose different requirements on a purchasing mechanism.
icml-2026-from-welfare-to-utility-genera.tldr: The paper designs budget-feasible purchasing mechanisms for welfare and buyer utility, with guarantees that depend on the objective and available cost information.

paragraphs: Multivariate time series contain several channels whose identities and relationships can vary across datasets. CHARM learns representations for this heterogeneous setting by combining sensor sequences with textual channel descriptions. Its Transformer encoder is equivariant to channel order, meaning that rearranging channels produces a corresponding rearrangement of the representation rather than changing their identities.

Training uses a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, which predicts in representation space, together with a loss encouraging embeddings to remain informative and stable over time. Latent prediction encourages robustness to sensor noise. A gating mechanism conditioned on descriptions also exposes learned relationships between channels, providing a way to interpret how the model combines their information.

The learned embeddings support strong results using only a linear probe for anomaly detection, classification, and forecasting over short and long horizons. The authors attribute most of the performance to the predictive objective and conditioning architecture. Text descriptions mainly function as channel identifiers that support generalization across datasets, clarifying their role within the multimodal system.
icml-2026-giving-sensors-a-voice-multimo.tldr: CHARM combines channel descriptions with predictive representation learning to produce useful, temporally stable embeddings for heterogeneous sensor data.

paragraphs: TANGO treats graph representation learning as a process in which node features evolve through a learned energy landscape. A learnable Lyapunov function assigns energy to the embeddings, and its gradient supplies a direction that does not increase that energy. This gives the feature dynamics a mathematical basis for stability.

Energy descent alone can provide limited movement in flat or poorly conditioned regions. TANGO adds a second component, learned through message passing, that moves features tangentially while preserving the energy value. The two components are orthogonal: one descends the energy landscape, while the other allows additional evolution without undoing that energy behavior.

This decomposition supports flexible dynamics and effective signal propagation in regions where descent is less useful. The framework is designed to help alleviate oversquashing and can work with different graph neural network backbones. Experiments report strong performance across node and graph classification and regression benchmarks. The findings support combining a learned stability structure with energy-preserving movement as a useful design for graph representations.
icml-2026-graph-neural-dynamics-via-lear.tldr: TANGO combines stable energy descent with learned energy-preserving flows to improve graph feature evolution and signal propagation.

paragraphs: Instance-wise feature selection identifies which inputs matter for each individual example. This can help explain labeled data or the predictions of a black-box model. A common approach trains a selector to choose features and a predictor to use them, but existing methods can suffer from information leakage and operations that are difficult to differentiate.

Hide&Seek jointly learns selection and prediction under a single objective. Its main change is to make feature removal continuous: it replaces a proportion of each feature instead of making an entirely discrete removal decision. That reformulation permits end-to-end differentiation, allowing the selector and predictor to be optimized together within the same training process.

The authors also gradually adjust the weight encouraging parsimonious feature use to stabilize training. They report that the resulting model avoids information leakage, trains quickly, and outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches across their experiments. The contribution connects an explanation mechanism to a practical optimization strategy: learning which features to retain becomes part of the differentiable prediction process.
icml-2026-hide-seek-learning-to-explain-.tldr: Hide&Seek learns per-example feature explanations through differentiable partial feature replacement, jointly training selection and prediction without information leakage.

paragraphs: Dual-encoder training with InfoNCE often uses other examples in the same mini-batch as negative examples. The learning signal depends on whether these negatives are challenging enough to distinguish from the correct match. When they are too easy, learning can quickly saturate, while explicitly mining harder negatives can be costly or depend on heuristics.

HOBIT improves this signal by changing which training examples appear together. At each epoch, it reorders examples using an optimization objective motivated by InfoNCE. The aim is to expose each query to negatives that are difficult, informative, and non-contradictory. Batch construction therefore becomes an explicit part of improving the contrastive learning objective.

The authors show that their objective is monotone and submodular, enabling a greedy algorithm with the standard approximately 1−1/e approximation guarantee. That guarantee concerns the batch optimization objective. Empirically, HOBIT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art batching approaches with negligible computational overhead. It also complements existing hard-negative mining, suggesting that choosing useful batches can add value even when negatives are already mined.
icml-2026-hobit-hardness-optimized-batch.tldr: HOBIT optimizes mini-batch composition to supply informative hard negatives, improving InfoNCE training with negligible reported overhead.

paragraphs: In partially observable reinforcement learning, extra information available during training can help a critic guide policy learning. Existing asymmetric actor-critic methods often give the critic the full environment state. This paper expands the framework to cases where training provides only selected state-dependent signals, making full-state access unnecessary for the proposed formulation.

The authors show that any such privileged signal can yield unbiased policy gradient estimates within their framework. This establishes admissibility, while leaving a separate question: which signals actually help learning most? They introduce two informativeness criteria to address that choice, one based on dependence that can be checked before training and another based on improvements in value prediction assessed afterward.

Experiments on partially observable benchmarks and synthetic environments show that carefully chosen signals can match or outperform full-state asymmetric baselines despite containing strictly less state information. The finding emphasizes selection rather than information quantity alone. A signal’s usefulness depends on how it supports the critic’s learning role, and the proposed tests provide ways to investigate that usefulness.
icml-2026-informed-asymmetric-actor-crit.tldr: Selected privileged training signals can support unbiased actor-critic learning and sometimes outperform full-state critics with less information.

paragraphs: Some learning problems require finding an ordering without being given the correct arrangement. Sorting can be guided by monotonicity, while jigsaw reconstruction can be guided by spatial continuity. Differentiable permutation methods make such learning possible by representing assignments with soft matrices that gradually approach discrete permutations.

The paper identifies a problem with using one global temperature to control that transition. Different assignments become certain at different times, so a single setting forces clear and ambiguous choices to sharpen together. The proposed entropy-adaptive Gumbel–Sinkhorn formulation instead adjusts temperature locally according to assignment uncertainty. Confident choices can become discrete earlier while uncertain ones retain room for exploration.

Experiments cover sorting, jigsaw reconstruction, and routing-style settings. Compared with fixed-temperature baselines, adaptive entropy control improves training stability and final permutation quality, particularly as problems become larger and assignments more ambiguous. The result supports allowing different parts of an ordering problem to settle at different rates, matching the optimization process to the uneven uncertainty that arises without supervision.
icml-2026-learning-permutation-from-stru.tldr: Locally adapting Gumbel–Sinkhorn temperatures to assignment uncertainty improves unsupervised permutation learning, especially for larger and more ambiguous problems.

paragraphs: A treatment allocation can benefit a population while still treating some patients who receive no benefit. This paper defines treatment risk as the proportion of treated patients in that group. Controlling this proportion matters because unnecessary treatment consumes resources and may expose patients to adverse effects without a corresponding benefit.

The learning challenge is that this risk generally cannot be uniquely determined from either randomized trial data or observational data. The paper therefore works in a partially identified setting, where the available evidence does not resolve the target quantity completely. This makes risk control a distinct requirement beyond simply learning an allocation with beneficial outcomes.

The authors propose a certifiable method that learns beneficial allocations while controlling treatment risk using finite samples. They illustrate it with simulated and real data. Its central contribution is to combine allocation learning with a risk-control guarantee despite incomplete identification. The guarantee concerns unnecessary treatment as defined in the paper, connecting the learning objective directly to how many treated patients may fail to benefit.
icml-2026-learning-treatment-allocations.tldr: The paper proposes finite-sample, certifiable learning of treatment allocations that controls unnecessary treatment despite partial identification of that risk.

paragraphs: As a context grows, softmax attention can spread weight across irrelevant tokens, weakening retrieval of the information that matters. Lowering the softmax temperature can sharpen attention, but it also creates vanishing-gradient problems that hinder learning. LUCID modifies attention to improve focus without relying on that low-temperature strategy.

Its preconditioner is derived from exponentiated similarities between keys and applied to attention probabilities. The construction minimizes overlap among keys in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, helping a query distinguish relevant keys within a large collection. The method retains the computational complexity of standard attention while changing the geometry underlying retrieval.

The authors evaluate approximately one-billion-parameter language models on contexts up to 128,000 tokens. They report significant gains on retrieval tasks from BABILong, RULER, SCROLLS, and LongBench, including improvements up to 18% on BABILong and 14% on RULER multi-needle performance over standard attention. These results support preconditioning as a way to improve long-context retrieval while avoiding the learning difficulties associated with lowering softmax temperature.
icml-2026-lucid-attention-with-precondit.tldr: LUCID preconditions attention using key similarities to improve long-context retrieval without lowering softmax temperature or changing computational complexity.

paragraphs: A diffusion model trained on noisy data learns from a distribution that differs from the clean distribution of interest. MAD modifies the sampling procedure to target noiseless samples in this setting. Its motivation comes from the manifold hypothesis: meaningful high-dimensional data is concentrated near a structure with fewer intrinsic dimensions.

The approach distinguishes small variations away from that structure from larger variations associated with meaningful data. It introduces an extended score designed to suppress the former while retaining the latter. In a simplified setting, the authors show that this score can reduce small variations to zero while leaving large variations mostly unchanged, providing a theoretical basis for the proposed behavior.

The extended score can be approximated efficiently from an approximation to the standard score, making the change implementable within inference. Demonstrations on toy problems, synthetic data, and real data show its effectiveness. The stated mechanism depends on the geometric distinction between noise and relevant variation, and the precise theoretical suppression result is established in the simplified setting.
icml-2026-mad-manifold-attracted-diffusi.tldr: MAD modifies diffusion sampling to suppress small off-manifold variations and generate cleaner samples from models trained on noisy data.

paragraphs: Score-based and flow-based models can represent complex action distributions, but generating actions through iterative sampling can be slow. In reinforcement learning, that delay becomes a computational bottleneck. Moment Matching Q-Learning addresses this problem by using distribution matching to support more efficient action sampling while maintaining policy performance.

The framework uses maximum mean discrepancy, a statistical comparison intended to match all orders of statistics between the original and target distributions. The authors state that strong regularization across these moment statistics guarantees distribution-level convergence for the conditional score function. They also report stability across various hyperparameter settings, connecting distribution matching to both the method’s theoretical behavior and practical training.

On several D4RL tasks, MoMa QL achieves greater computational efficiency with comparable or competitive performance. It also reports superior results in offline-to-online reinforcement learning when accelerating action sampling for flow-based policies. In that setting, the authors attribute the gains to faster and stronger adaptation during interactive fine-tuning, linking sampling efficiency to the ability to improve through online experience.
icml-2026-moment-matching-q-learning-1a8.tldr: MoMa QL uses moment-based distribution matching to accelerate generative-policy action sampling and improve offline-to-online adaptation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: State tracking requires a sequence model to maintain the information needed as a sequence unfolds. Earlier concerns about Transformers often centered on generalizing beyond the training distribution, such as processing longer sequences. This paper examines whether difficulties also arise when training and evaluation distributions match.

A large-scale experimental study compares the data efficiency of Transformers and recurrent neural networks under multiple supervision regimes. As state spaces and sequence lengths grow, the training data required by Transformers increases much more rapidly. The authors also examine whether learning at one sequence length supports performance at another, probing how broadly the learned tracking mechanism is reused.

In the evaluated settings, Transformers show negligible or even detrimental sharing across lengths, consistent with learning separate length-specific solutions. Recurrent models show effective shared learning: data at one length can help at others. These findings place the challenge within ordinary in-distribution learning as well as extrapolation. They indicate that matching the evaluation distribution does not remove the observed differences in state-tracking data efficiency.
icml-2026-on-the-induction-bias-in-seque.tldr: Experiments find that Transformers learn state tracking less data-efficiently than recurrent models, even when training and evaluation distributions match.

paragraphs: Reasoning about an environment can require both causal understanding and the ability to handle unfamiliar combinations of objects. This paper develops relational structural causal models for settings where the objects and relationships themselves vary. The framework extends causal modeling to support questions about interventions and counterfactuals in these changing configurations.

The authors first establish an identification obstacle: without additional assumptions, even observational queries about unseen object combinations cannot necessarily be determined, and causal queries face the same problem. They introduce relational causal graphs and symbolic identification criteria to specify when such questions can be answered, including settings with unobserved confounding.

The paper then proposes relational neural causal models as a provably correct approach within the developed framework. On simulated traffic scenes with varying cars, signals, and pedestrians, these models outperform non-relational baselines. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary parts of the problem: identifying when the evidence supports an answer and constructing a model that can exploit relational structure to answer across changing object combinations.
icml-2026-relational-structural-causal-m.tldr: Relational causal models establish conditions for answering queries about unseen object combinations and outperform non-relational baselines in simulated traffic scenes.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts architectures are widely used in large language models, but their accuracy relative to computation and parameter count remains a design question. This paper revisits that question through hardware-software co-design, examining how architectural choices interact with the practical demands of inference.

The authors characterize bottlenecks across both offline execution, where high throughput matters, and online serving, where response latency is critical. They use those findings and systematic design exploration to develop LatentMoE, an architecture aimed at improving accuracy per unit of compute. The study combines empirical exploration with theoretical analysis to assess the resulting efficiency trade-offs.

Experiments extend to models with 95 billion parameters and training horizons exceeding one trillion tokens. Within this exploration, LatentMoE consistently improves accuracy per FLOP and per parameter over standard MoE architectures. The abstract also reports adoption in Nemotron-3 Super and Ultra and scaling to larger regimes. The central finding is that reconsidering MoE design around deployment bottlenecks can improve the accuracy obtained from a given computational or parameter budget.
icml-2026-revisiting-efficiencyaccuracy-.tldr: LatentMoE improves accuracy per FLOP and per parameter over standard MoE designs in a large empirical and theoretical architecture study.

paragraphs: An assistive agent should help a person achieve their objectives while leaving them control over important decisions. The paper argues that imitation and reward-based fine-tuning can encourage agents to complete tasks independently. It proposes human empowerment as a training objective, defined as the person’s ability to bring about desired changes in the environment.

The resulting method, Empower, fine-tunes language models using only offline examples of human-written text. Its self-supervised formulation does not require human feedback or verifiable rewards for training. This makes the desired role of the assistant explicit in the objective: assistance should support the human’s ability to act and influence outcomes.

An 18-person user study compares the empowerment assistant with a strong baseline. Participants prefer it 78% of the time, with a reported p-value of 0.015, and its acceptance rate is 31% higher. These findings support the approach in the studied interaction setting. The paper offers empowerment maximization as a framework for training useful assistants around human agency, supported by the reported user preferences.
icml-2026-training-llm-agents-to-empower.tldr: Empower fine-tunes assistants to support human agency using offline text, earning 78% preference in an 18-person comparison study.

paragraphs: Machine learning approaches to the Traveling Salesperson Problem often predict a heatmap indicating which edges are likely to belong to an optimal tour. Those predictions do not themselves constitute a tour. Turning them into a complete solution remains a difficult and potentially expensive part of the overall optimization process.

This paper proposes algorithms for that conversion step and gives guarantees tied explicitly to prediction quality. The approximation ratio is expressed as 1 + 2η/OPT, where η is the L1 distance between the predicted heatmap and an optimal tour, and OPT is the optimal tour cost. As the prediction error decreases relative to OPT, the stated bound approaches one.

The contribution fits the algorithms-with-predictions approach: learned information guides an algorithm whose solution quality can be bounded in terms of that information’s accuracy. The authors also compare their approach experimentally with earlier methods lacking such explicit guarantees. The abstract’s stated result is the prediction-dependent bound, which gives a direct relationship between heatmap accuracy and the quality guaranteed for the resulting tour.
icml-2026-tsp-with-predictions-heatmap-t.tldr: The paper converts predicted TSP edge heatmaps into tours with approximation guarantees that improve as prediction error decreases.

paragraphs: Removing a class from a model can leave detectable traces in how it assigns probabilities to other classes. This paper argues that class-unlearning evaluations miss leakage when they ignore relationships among classes. Its Class Membership Inference Attack detects unlearned samples using the model’s probabilities for neighboring classes.

The authors find vulnerability to this attack across multiple datasets and introduce Tilted REWeighting, or TREW, to mitigate it. TREW estimates similarities between classes and adjusts the model’s distribution to approximate how a model retrained from scratch would distribute probabilities over remaining classes for forget-class inputs. Fine-tuning then encourages the model to match this adjusted target.

Across multiple benchmarks, TREW matches or exceeds existing methods on prior unlearning metrics while addressing the newly exposed leakage. On CIFAR-10, it reduces the gap from retrained models by 19% for U-LiRA and 46% for CMIA compared with the state-of-the-art method in each category. The findings show why evaluation should consider the pattern of remaining-class probabilities when assessing whether class information persists.
icml-2026-unlearning-isnt-forgetting-rev.tldr: A new attack exposes class information retained after unlearning, and TREW mitigates it by approximating retrained models’ remaining-class predictions.

paragraphs: Entropic optimal transport provides a way to translate between distributions in continuous spaces. For quadratic transport costs, a commonly used weak dual objective depends on one potential but contains a difficult log-partition term. Existing approaches handle it through restricted families with tractable normalization or flexible neural models requiring simulation-based training.

VarEOT replaces this computational obstacle with an exact variational reformulation. It expresses the log-partition term as a tractable minimization over an additional positive normalizer. The resulting objective is differentiable and can be optimized with stochastic gradients, avoiding the need for MCMC simulations during training. The reformulation changes how the objective is optimized while preserving its exact mathematical basis.

The authors provide finite-sample generalization bounds and approximation results under universal function approximation. Experiments on synthetic data and unpaired image translation show competitive or improved translation quality. Comparisons among solvers using the same weak dual objective further support the proposed optimization principle, helping connect the observed benefits to the reformulation rather than simply to choosing a different transport objective.
icml-2026-variational-entropic-optimal-t.tldr: VarEOT exactly reformulates a difficult normalization term to train entropic transport models with stochastic gradients and no required MCMC training simulations.
